speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Currently, the regulation of the food industry is divided among three public sector agencies.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Agri-Food and Veterinary Authority (AVA) regulates food safety before retail during import, local production and manufacturing.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The National Environment Agency (NEA) regulates food hygiene at the retail level.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Analysis of food samples is carried out at laboratories under the Health Sciences Authority (HSA).

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Singapore is not the first country to adopt a farm-to-fork model.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have studied other countries like Ireland, where a single agency is responsible for food safety along the entire food supply chain.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There are merits to consolidate the responsibilities for food safety and security into a single agency.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One, it emphasises the high priority and commitment that the Government places on food safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Two, it allows uniform application of measures, faster response, and more efficient and effective use of resources and expertise.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: NEA will, however, continue to develop and manage hawker centres as our community dining rooms.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This arrangement will enable sharper focus by SFA and NEA in their respective roles vis-a-vis hawker centres.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: HPB will continue to promote the consumption of healthy food.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: SFA will support them from the food safety angle.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: AVA’s remaining non-food plant and animal-related functions will be transferred to the National Parks Board (NParks) via the National Parks Board (Amendment) Bill 2019.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Minister for National Development will explain this transfer during the Second Reading of the National Parks Board (Amendment) Bill 2019.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have worked hard to ensure Singapore’s food safety and security over the decades.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is critical because Singapore depends heavily on food imports.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is testimony to the hard work by generations of our staff since AVA’s early days at the Primary Production Department in pre-Independence Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have done well but cannot take the current situation for granted.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The agriculture and food, or agri-food, landscape is changing rapidly.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Global food demand is also projected to rise by 60% as incomes rise in developing countries, leading to greater demand for meat and proteins.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Vital resources to meet the increased food demand, such as water and energy, are increasingly scarce.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The World Bank estimates that agriculture accounts for 70% of global water consumption but one-third of the world’s population lives in water-stressed areas.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over the longer-term horizon, too, climate change will exacerbate these threats.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Extreme temperatures, droughts and floods from rising sea levels will affect production yield.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation estimates widespread declines in crop yields of between 10% and 25% by 2050 due to climate change impacts.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines forecasts a 20% reduction in Asian rice yields for every degree of temperature rise.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Rice becomes sterile if exposed to temperatures above 35oC for more than one hour during flowering.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: A heat wave during flowering season, like in Australia right now, would wipe out the entire year’s crop.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Scientists from various disciplines all mark 2050 as a watershed year when projected increase in population intersects with severe decline in crop yields due to unmitigated climate change.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Competition for water, energy and, consequently, food, will escalate conflicts if not mitigated.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, right here in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), one of my counterparts shared with me that the impact of climate change is already being felt and has caused more frequent and severe droughts and floods in the Mekong River Delta, which is the "rice bowl" of Asia.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The 2007 and 2008 global food crises, which stemmed from various factors, including droughts and rising oil prices, triggered spikes in food prices worldwide, and even led to street protests in Indonesia and Bangladesh.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Food producing countries like India and Brazil introduced export bans.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These impacts were felt in Singapore in the form of increased prices.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We also need to manage the risks from the growing complexity in global food supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our food undergoes multiple processes involving many players in different countries, before reaching our tables.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, the frozen pizza in our supermarkets can have more than 10 ingredients from different sources.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The pineapple could have been grown in the Philippines, the ham brined in Australia, the tomato sauce canned in the US and the flour milled in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This simple example highlights the confluence of food supply and food safety, and the challenges we face.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: On the one hand, we get to enjoy a wide range of ingredients and cuisine.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: On the other hand, complex global supply chains increase the potential points of failure where contamination can enter the food chain.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This makes it more difficult to identify the source of the problems when they occur.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Was the cause of a food poisoning incident due to poor hygiene in the restaurant or hotel?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Could it have been due to high levels of pesticides on the raw ingredients?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Contaminants introduced in the manufacturing process of packing and canning?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Or deterioration in quality and safety during transportation?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Complex supply chains will evolve as climate change affects production.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Epidemiology has to keep up with changes in the survival and transmission patterns of food-borne diseases.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In Singapore, Government agencies have worked well together to address food safety and security, and we have a strong reputation.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But we must ensure that our food safety and security regime is well ahead of the curve.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, in the scenario of a food poisoning incident, a single team will oversee the entire food supply chain and manage investigations.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Starting from the accreditation of overseas farms, to import, to intermediate processing by central kitchens and retailers, and finally to the proper storage and preparation at the retail outlet.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will allow SFA to respond more promptly to trace the source of contamination.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Strategic advantages to secure our food supply, transform our agri-food industry, develop our local enterprises, and provide good jobs to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Just like how we have turned our vulnerability in water into opportunity.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: First, new food production methods and techniques are emerging at an unprecedented pace.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Modern food production has become more productive, sustainable and resilient to climate change.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We can learn from others around the world how they leverage their strengths and overcome their constraints.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The United Arab Emirates enjoys cheap and abundant energy but struggles with a hot and dry desert climate where water is extremely scarce.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: On the other hand, water is abundant in the Netherlands, but energy is expensive and scarce.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I visited a tomato farm in Dubai last month, which channels waste carbon dioxide from air-conditioning back into the glasshouse to boost the plants' growth.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To reduce water use, the farm recirculates the nutrient solution used to feed the crops.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The farm is able to produce tomatoes at high yields consistently throughout the year, even when the temperature outside reaches 50oC.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Last year, I visited Wageningen University and Research in the Netherlands and was impressed by their innovation in greenhouse technologies to reduce energy consumption in the cultivation of tomatoes.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Their target is to produce net-zero energy greenhouses.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Singapore suffers scarcity at both extremes – scarcity of water and energy.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must develop our own approach to agriculture, which accounts for our deficiencies in water and energy and, to add to this complexity, also land.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Technology now allows us to solve this conundrum.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our future farms will be different from the farms that we are familiar with today.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Rather than backbreaking physical toil under the sun, new-age farmers will work indoors in an environmentally controlled enclosure, much like the Domes at the Gardens by the Bay.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Instead of shovels and hoes, they will operate computers controlling autonomous robots that plant seeds and harvest crops.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With the right crops, these farms operate at much higher productivity and can sustain good jobs.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, such technological innovations apply not to just land-based farming, but even aquaculture where we can increase the yield and improve the quality of our local seafood.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The working environments will be almost indistinguishable from the offices or automated production lines many of us work in today.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must seize opportunities in the agri-food sector to further enhance our food supply resilience.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must sow the seeds now for Singapore’s development into an agri-food hub.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In time to come, we will harvest the benefits – a strong stable of local enterprises which can export sustainable urban food solutions to cities around the world, good jobs which will appeal to Singaporeans, and a secure supply of safe food for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Second, the emergence of new and novel food products.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These have the potential to provide us with a safe and sustainable supply of food, without compromising on taste or health.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One example is plant-based protein with meat-like texture and taste from companies, such as Beyond Meat and Impossible Foods.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These new food products have a smaller environmental footprint, compared to conventional meat products, and could potentially be scaled up to meet future food demand.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Another example is the cultivation of insects, such as the black soldier fly, for animal feed.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will require us to make a conscious effort to position Singapore as an agri-food hub – from facilitative regulations that encourage innovation, to creating the necessary research and development ecosystem and growing a pipeline of Singaporean talent.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clauses 5 and 6 lay out SFA's functions and powers, which are drawn from existing provisions in the AVA and NEA Acts.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These include developing the food industry, regulating food safety across the supply chain, and regulating street hawking and trade fairs.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Parts 3 to 6 cover governance matters, such as the appointment and decision-making procedures of SFA, personnel matters, including the appointment of the Chief Executive, and financial provisions of SFA.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The provisions are aligned with the requirements in the Public Sector (Governance) Act 2018.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Part 7 of the Bill contains miscellaneous provisions necessary for the administration and enforcement of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In particular, clause 43 will protect against the improper use of accreditation, certification and inspection marks that are administered by SFA.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This includes schemes to be administered by SFA, and third-party testing, inspection and certification services.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is to ensure that all licensees and products carrying such marks meet SFA's stringent standards, in order to facilitate the growth of the local farming and food export industries.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Once the transfer takes place, the AVA Act will be repealed by clause 55.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Part 9 of the Bill makes related and consequential amendments to other Acts.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: First, with the consolidation of food safety functions in a single agency, and the transfer of non-food related functions to NParks, some pieces of legislation become obsolete and are being repealed.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clause 59 will repeal provisions in the Fisheries Act relating to the prohibition, regulation or control of piranha or any other dangerous species of fish.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: NParks will take over this function from AVA and draw powers from the Animals and Birds Act.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The regulation of stage shows under EPHA will be abolished, as this is already regulated under the Public Entertainments Act administered by the Singapore Police Force.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Next, clause 62 amends the functions of the NEA in the NEA Act to remove food-related functions since these are transferred to SFA.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clauses 57 and 61 further make consequential amendments to the EPHA and the Infectious Diseases Act (IDA) respectively to transfer powers from NEA's Director-General of Public Health to SFA's Director-General, Food Administration (DG FA).

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: DG FA will administer Parts 4 and 9 of EPHA that relate to the safety of food and drinking water for consumption, and the licensing of retail food establishments, markets and hawkers.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: DG FA will also administer sections 38 and 39 of IDA which relate to the supply of food and water to vessels.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The EPHA will also be amended to provide powers to both the Director-General of Public Health and DG FA, to modify the conditions of a licence after giving notice to the licensee.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is to facilitate further reviews to extend the duration of licences issued under EPHA.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clauses 58, 59, 64 and 65 make consequential amendments to the Feeding Stuffs Act, Fisheries Act, Sale of Food Act and Wholesome Meat and Fish Act respectively to transfer the administration of the Acts from the Director-General, Agri-Food and Veterinary Services to DG FA.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clauses 59, 64 and 65 make other related amendments to the Fisheries Act, Sale of Food Act, and Wholesome Meat and Fish Act, respectively to provide the Minister to make regulations requiring records on imports and food stocks to be kept and supplied to DG FA upon request.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will allow DG FA to monitor the supply of fish, meat and other food items to ensure a secure and reliable food supply in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These powers will extend to food businesses, fisheries and persons involved in fish cultivation, and importers of food in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: DG FA will also be empowered to take into consideration the ability of importers of food items, such as meat and fish, to provide a secure and reliable supply when granting licences, and to impose licence conditions to this end.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will enable DG FA to work with importers of key food items to adopt plans, including preventive strategies, to mitigate the impact for supply disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will not be the last time that Singapore faces possible disruption to our food imports.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must, therefore, continue to diversify our food import sources and not be over-reliant on any single source.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: SFA will also continue to partner other Government agencies to ensure basic food items remain affordable.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clause 60 amends the HPB Act to better delineate the food functions between SFA and HPB.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: HPB's role is to encourage and facilitate healthier food choices in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clause 63 abolishes the exclusion of land used for agriculture from being treated as a development, for the purposes of the Planning Act.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This paves the way for SFA to work closely with the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) to better develop land in Singapore that will be used for agricultural purposes.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The implementation details will be finalised by the Government agencies supporting the task force.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As in other Bills, the Minister is conferred power to make regulations setting out additional provisions of a saving or transitional nature.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are food and beverage (F&B) staff overworked, resulting in lapses in food handling hygiene?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These are common concerns that people would raise when they see yet another news report concerning food safety lapses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In truth, the food landscape in Singapore and around the world is evolving rapidly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Globalisation and new business models have made food supply chains more complex than ever.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: International brand names are setting up restaurants on our sunny island and they are also flying in raw ingredients from overseas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Climate changes and disasters disrupt the supply of food ingredients, pressuring businesses to turn to alternative sources.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps the pressure to deliver under disruption may have compromised some safety procedures.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Domestically, more young people are turning to entrepreneurship and, considering Singaporeans' passion for food, it is not surprising that cafes and eateries are popular business choices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With the gig economy becoming increasingly mainstream, we are also seeing more freelancers making use of their talents to become home bakers and private chefs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Food deliveries are becoming the norm for F&B establishments, from hawker centres to restaurants to grocery retailers, to deliver consumers' meals.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, this adds additional challenges to the food safety process – packaging, exposure to outdoor temperatures and with more people involved in handling of the food.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These are all additional matters to consider in food safety management.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is being done by overseeing food safety across the entire food supply chain from farm-to-fork.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: SFA has promised to harmonise regulatory and enforcement processes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hopefully, in doing so, there can be better coordination for food-related issues, product tracing and recall, as well as engagement of stakeholders and members of the public.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, SFA will require adequate manpower and resources to implement such a large-scale process.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How will technology be applicable to make the process more efficient?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Meanwhile, I do not think it is practical to rely on SFA to manage every aspect of food safety for all F&B services and businesses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The onus is on business owners to provide their customers with meals that are safe to consume.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the newly established SFA will work closely with these businesses, including freelancers, to provide them with the education and resources they would require, staying abreast with food safety management requirements.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, perhaps it would be timely to review the mandatory basic food hygiene courses that food handlers are required to undergo, and the frequency of the mandatory refresher course could be increased as well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are fortunate that our country is free from natural disasters due to our prime location.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, that does not absolve us from being at the mercy of natural disasters and disease outbreaks that hit other countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Most of our food products are imported from other countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We get hit by whatever shortages and price hikes that impact on our importers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With the world climate becoming increasingly unpredictable, it is sensible of SFA to consider food security among its priorities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A key food security strategy is to diversify our food supply sources, much like what we did with our water supply.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Moreover, the ability to collect food-related data from the industry will help us to better prepare and plan for food supply disruptions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, while this is a good strategy, this could mean additional burdens on importers of vital food items to come up with the relevant diversification strategies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will SFA provide any form of assistance to these importers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that AVA has helped to organise overseas food sourcing trips and match importers to suppliers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will SFA continue this and possibly even enhance it?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Happily, there has been growing interest in farming among young Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are farmers’ market events where one can purchase locally grown organic produce.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are hearing more about Singaporeans volunteering in community gardens or growing their own indoor produce.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon South, we encourage residents to take part in community gardening.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One such active resident is Mr Ong Choon Yeow, who was featured in the Straits Times recently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Ong said that he rarely buys vegetables and he gets his vegetables from the community garden on top of our multi-storey carpark besides our Community Club because that multi-storey carpark, the top level, is seldom used.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, we converted that to a community garden for residents to plant vegetables.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure that if we can systematically harness every inch of our soil, like what we do for water, we can achieve amazing results.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am looking forward to hearing about the specific plans that SFA has in place to achieve this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We will need to have the relevant talent for sure, and I trust that SFA will be working with educational institutions to open up new education pathways for those who are interested in food science, agriculture and other relevant disciplines.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: By developing a new sector, we can expect to open up a new job market for Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And for Singaporeans who have a passion for agriculture but feel inhibited by the lack of demand, they can take heart that they may soon be able to work towards fulfilling their dreams of going professional right here on home ground.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We can look forward to better safety protocols with regard to our food, and opportunities to grow our capabilities and extend our relevance in the global market.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The food industry is facing tremendous challenges, such as the popularisation of food delivery services and global warming.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope SFA can introduce courses in urban farming, hence providing a new career choice for Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NEA’s food hygiene arm, which has been the frontline agency dealing with the recent spate of food poisoning cases, as well as HSA’s food safety lab, will be subsumed under SFA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, SFA will be in charge of food safety and also national food security.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: AVA’s remit of regulating and nurturing the farming sector will also, presumably, come under the new SFA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill creates a one-stop shop for food licensing as well as food safety inspection and response.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the fact that one agency is licensing central kitchens and caterers means that businesses may be able to save costs by not duplicating locations for these distinct facilities, cost-savings which may be passed on to consumers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do, however, have several questions and comments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before I continue, I declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer of a research consultancy that undertakes studies in the agri-food space, among other sectors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most of these deaths are caused by pathogens, such as salmonella, E coli and norovirus, and the majority of lives lost are in Africa and Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And that case was the tragic death of the late Mr Fadli Saleh in November last year, seemingly as a result of a mass food poisoning incident.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There were five reported mass poisoning incidents in the last quarter of 2018 alone.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the end of the day, I suspect that the problem of unsafe food from food-service outlets may come down, in many cases, to the human factor – an employee showing up for work when he or she is ill, a supervisor willing to turn a blind eye to that, individual negligence in food handling practices and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the new SFA consider taking a long hard look at the entire profession of food handlers, which is to say, all those involved in food preparation and handling, to understand if their conditions of work, training, compensation and workplace environment are in line with global norms?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If, and I stress if, poor compensation, career prospects and treatment by employers are persistently found in this industry, while it does not absolve individuals from individual responsibility, it would perhaps explain the root causes which need to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would urge the new SFA to look deeply into the conditions of work of food handlers, including their economic conditions, to understand if there is more we could be doing to address the root causes of such incidents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having said that, penalties, enforcement and deterrence are important parts of a healthy food safety ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, I note that some larger and more organised food-service outlets have their own corporate whistleblower hotlines, though I very much doubt that the same can be said for most companies in the industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the very least, would the Government consider instituting protections for whistleblowers who identify legitimate food safety problems and enable their rectification?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the United States (US), laws exist to protect employees who blow the whistle on food safety violations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For instance, under the US Food and Drug Administration, the Food Safety Modernization Act of 2011 has provisions against retaliation toward whistleblowers by food businesses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The United Kingdom (UK), China and other countries also have similar laws and regulations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to confirm that, in addition to sample checks of imports, SFA will also conduct proactive surveillance of global news reports to identify potential food safety dangers among global food exporters who are exporting food into Singapore, so that proactive preventive action can be taken.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This issue came to the fore in the recent case about the possibility of needles in strawberries imported from Australia.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I would like to ask if the Government currently publishes the results of its sample food safety checks in aggregate form, that is to say, without naming specific establishments, as this will serve as a useful barometer on how well we are doing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this is not currently being done, can this be considered?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the US regularly publishes the results of its national residue programme that inspects meat, poultry and egg products for chemical residues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, on the subject of food safety, I would urge SFA to look into food labelling requirements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can nutrition labelling be made mandatory rather than being only recommended?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, the Handbook on Nutrition Labelling does not list sugar as a core nutrient that is recommended to be listed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Added sugar should be called out on labels so as not to deter consumption of natural sugars in healthy food products like fruit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The inclusion of added sugars on the label can be a tool in the effort to educate the public about the health risks associated with excessive consumption of refined, added sugars.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to speak about the farming sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the Government press release announcing this Bill, Minister for the Environment and Water Resources Mr Masagos Zulkifli said, and I quote: "The formation of SFA is timely as Singapore aims to turn our food challenges into opportunities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SFA will work closely with industry partners to develop new solutions and products...

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (such as) climate resilient farming solutions and advanced food manufacturing techniques.” SFA, I assume, will take over the role of nurturing and regulating the farm sector in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a subject I have spoken about in Parliament several times before and I would like to urge SFA to focus on several key areas in this effort.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No doubt, it is unlikely that we will ever produce all our food domestically, at least in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But with recent advances in indoor farming technology and the presence of Government support, is there room to raise these targets, using the tool of the APF to support local farms in raising output?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, I hope SFA will also address a number of the issues I have spoken about in Parliament in the past relating to the farming sector – the length of leases where there has been some improvement, a level playing field for local startups and farm tenders, and the need to promote adoption of effective insurance against both natural and man-made disasters.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, an emerging trend in the global food industry is that of micro-brands, which is to say, startups developing their own unique food products and selling these online.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A long tail of 20,000 companies below the top 100 produced half of all growth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These startups sell all manner of food products, from Greek yoghurt and micro-brewed beer to allergy-friendly snacks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important that our regulation and inspection framework keeps abreast of this trend and ensures food safety in these supply chains, both during production and delivery.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, we should embrace relevant global trends.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Food micro-brands can help increase choice and reduce cost, which micro-brands have helped bring about in other non-food categories like, for example, mattresses and shaving razors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, food micro-brands could create good jobs in Singapore and could be a domain for fruitful local entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The creation of SFA is a timely natural evolution of existing governance mechanisms to safeguard Singapore’s food security in an era of global food uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I wish to speak on three areas: food safety, food security and food sustainability.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: On food safety, Singapore have developed a world-class food safety system that is comprehensive and robust in responding to real-world shocks.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, in Australia, widespread panic was sparked when needles were found in strawberries.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In 2013, horse meat was discovered in products falsely advertised as beef in the UK.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, through an immutable, distributed ledger system, the authorities can keep track of suppliers and food items as they move down the supply chain.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This would allow the authorities to quickly trace the origins of contaminated food items to their sources and hold the right parties accountable for any lapses, mitigating the impact of contaminated or sabotaged food.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: With the rise of e-commerce, many Singaporeans are purchasing food-related products from overseas sources and having it directly shipped to them.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In 2018, Singapore was ranked No 1 in the Global Food Security Index formulated by the Economist Intelligence Unit.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This is a commendable feat for a country that imports about 90% of its food.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is also a testimony to the efficacy of our sound policies, tools and governance structures that have securitised food resources over the years.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must not rest on our laurels and take for granted the access to affordable and nutritious food that we enjoy now.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Our reliance on global food supplies to meet the needs of our people makes us susceptible to global price volatility.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The global food crisis of 2008 highlighted our vulnerability in being import-dependent.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The need to ensure access to affordable and safe food has emerged as a key policy agenda for many nations, as socioeconomic, climatic, demographic and political conditions shift over time.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As such, I would like to seek the Minister’s clarifications on the measures that will be undertaken to mitigate the volatility in future food prices due to supply disruptions.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Also, what are the requirements that will be introduced for importers of key food items to mitigate the impact of supply disruptions?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Future initiatives could also include public campaigns to educate the masses on measures, such as increasing the public’s resilience to food supply disruptions, either by encouraging stockpiling of food in homes or by shaping consumers’ willingness to switch to substitutes in times of shortages.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: On food sustainability, today, less than 1% of Singapore’s land is used for agriculture.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Modern agrotechnology is opening up new opportunities for small countries like Singapore, making it possible to produce significant amounts of food without delegating huge amounts of land and labour.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, from my interactions with the agro-industry players, there are still challenges that they face in adopting such technologies.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Despite being in the high-growth agrotech business, they were still deemed to be in the farming business.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Ministry can look into formulating a mechanism to differentiate the various farm types in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Besides agrotech farms, we should be more creative in the use of our limited space by collaborating with urban planners and communities to integrate urban agriculture into the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to cite the example of a sustainable urban farming model – the Citizen Farm.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The farm was piloted in the housing estate of Queenstown in 2016.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: A dilapidated, abandoned former prison along Jalan Penjara was transformed into a closed-loop urban farming system that integrated natural systems with modern technology.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond its use of technology and innovation, the farm had its foundations in a social enterprise model, with the aim of connecting communities through farm spaces.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Smaller startup technologies and innovations were also encouraged in the farms.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: These included indoor microgreen harvesting, mushroom farming and an indoor fish farm, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, the dilapidated, abandoned former prison was transformed into a thriving urban farming model.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The development of the Citizen Farm not only showcased the viability of small-scale urban farming setups in Singapore, but also highlighted the potential to convert underused, marginal land for interim purposes.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, these farming models are designed to be moveable and, therefore, can be easily adapted to various spaces.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Such setups could help to supplement local food production.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, these setups also provide much-needed spaces for startups to explore innovations in the agrotechnology sector.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, we can also look up to Japan as an example for how urban farming can be expanded and integrated into the life of our city.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, creativity and flexibility go a long way in maximising the potential of underused spaces.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to the Bill, I would like to seek clarification on section 5J regarding the role of SFA.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Given SFA's role as the main regulator on all matters relating to food, from farm to fork, how does it concurrently intend to play a role in promoting and developing the food industry, and would there be an overlap with Enterprise Singapore?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: SFA can serve as a good example of how both regulatory and industry promotion functions sit within a single agency, allowing not just more pro-enterprise outcomes, but greater agility in serving the needs of the industry.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: With the rapid progression of food and agriculture technologies, and an increasing global demand for food, this is an opportunity for Singapore to emerge as a forerunner in sustainable urban food solutions while fully meeting local needs.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore’s agriculture sector has evolved over time through efforts to optimise, adapt and strengthen food security.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: But the potential remains for us to do more, particularly in coming times.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Our water scarcity pushed us to develop the water treatment and management industry, transforming a threat into an opportunity and to develop strategic advantage.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, with food, we should aspire to create a Singapore Food Story, to establish Singapore as a recognised centre for food in the region, and even in the world.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: With optimism and encouragement, Mr Speaker, I support this Bill.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is about (a) availability of food, either from local or global sources; (b) accessibility of food by Singapore consumers through established supply chain networks; (c) affordability of food for consumers and people and (d) safety and nutrition standards of the food available for Singapore consumers.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, they also employ a large number of employees, and it is an important business, indeed.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Despite various constraints, such as scarcity of land, traditional agriculture and food farms as well as competing economic needs, we must continue to deliver safe, affordable and uninterrupted food supply for our people.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And one of the most important fundamental steps for a new agency is to get the basics working right.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With a dedicated agency overseeing our food safety and standards now, it is hoped that we can manage the challenges better, handle lapses more efficiently and effectively in a more coordinated fashion.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This includes, of course, food-borne disease outbreaks, through tighter controls and checking mechanisms, and engagement of the various stakeholders and the public as well.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We hope for better oversight and surveillance in general.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What newer areas of food supply and research can we expect to see?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will there be a focus on food diagnostics and development, the latter being one area that can address the food challenges a small urban country like Singapore will face?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, as there are now six institutions offering Food Science and Technology courses, that is, the National University of Singapore (NUS), Nanyang Polytechnic, Tampines Polytechnic, Singapore Polytechnic, the Singapore Hotel Association Training and Education Centre Institution and the AEC College, can you also share with us their programmes and curriculum as I feel that there needs to be a dynamic view of their education in order to stay relevant and even address Singapore's food needs?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How can these institutions work with the National Centre for Food Science (NCFS) in terms of supporting attachments, projects, scholarships, new innovative ideas and so on?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is going to be an important area that we will have to look towards the future.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One other institution, the WIL @ NUS, which has a lab by Wilmar International, opened in June 2018.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What is the progress in the work conducted?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This would include themes like newer food choices, specific nutrition for the elderly and seniors and healthier versions.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, we hope to be able to hear on some of the developments with these institutions.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In line with this, Singapore has a strategic location and position to attract more global and food R&D companies here.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our pro-innovation climate will, of course, be attractive to this as well.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What are the outcomes thus far and how is the progress?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I see this programme becoming more important in the coming years and, under SFA, we hope there will be more publicity on this programme and also recruitment of people and non-government organisations which are interested in having healthier food choices into the future as we look towards healthier ageing also.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With the new agency, how will the relationship with food industries and food businesses be strengthened?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They are the important partners who need to be engaged.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, therefore, it is really important that we have focus group discussions and also apprise them of the developments with this new agency.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The networks must be established, but we must also bear in mind the ringfencing of the security of our food resources and sources is important.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is because in this age of terrorism, food can serve as a source of targeted widespread terrorist type attacks to impact large numbers of people at one time, and we must ensure vigilance at all times.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, even with diversification, we need to maintain surveillance and monitoring and must never let our guard down.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our food safety network and framework must remain up to date and robust.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As a very small nation, changes in world food production, trade, food safety and supply will, of course, affect us.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But it also tests our resilience, our food innovation capabilities and security.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And with this new Bill, Sir, I definitely think we are going in the right direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Economist Intelligence Unit, which publishes the Index, cited Singapore's access to cheap, safe and nutritious food as the reason.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the Unit also noted that Singapore is most vulnerable to potential disruptions to our food supply due to climate change and natural resource risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When these risks were taken into account, our position in the Index would slip to 16th.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Establishing the SFA at this juncture is, therefore, a timely move to address these risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague Mr Leon Perera had addressed the food security and safety issues that SFA will be chiefly concerned with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For my part, I would like to raise what I believe are two important functions that SFA can and should perform, given its powers and position.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These two functions are, one, mitigating rising food prices that fuel increases in cost of living and, two, addressing household food insecurity within the country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first function is the mitigation of rising food prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At first glance, rising food prices do not discriminate among the rich, the poor and the middle-income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, rising food prices affect lower- and middle-income households disproportionately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the top 20% of households, food expenses make up only 6%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that any increase in food prices would have doubled the effect on the budget of poorer households, compared to richer households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rising food prices have been a regular concern of this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There have been many questions raised on this by Members.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This reflected the experience and concerns of ordinary Singaporeans, which were reported in the press.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, Minister Chan also said this increase was mitigated by other import sources, the prices of which remained stable or declined by up to 7%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On average, thus, the local retail price of eggs only increased around 4%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The big differences in percentages actually pose a mathematical puzzle worthy of a Primary School Leaving Examination question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I suspect the 50% increase is for the cheaper eggs imported by land and sea transport from neighbouring countries, and the other sources are much more expensive eggs air-flown from Australia and New Zealand and other places.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, the average retail price did not seem to have increased much.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The more important point here is that the low average rise in the price of eggs conceal the fact that the lower-income households are disproportionately affected by the 50% increase in the price of cheaper eggs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, Minister Chan's answer points to how rising food prices can be mitigated by strategies targeted at our food supply sources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He said, quote, "we must continually and consciously diversify our supply sources and supply chains to avoid being held ransom by the discontinuity in any particular supply source or disruption to any supply chain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This includes sourcing from different countries and building up a certain amount of local capacities where we can and when it makes economic sense." The proposed SFA will be in a good position to do just this, to diversify our food supply sources to avoid disruption and to build up local food production capacity to mitigate price increases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SFA could perform this function indirectly or directly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As listed in the Bill, one of the SFA's functions is to collect data on food supply and analyse them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another is to conduct research on food supply, and yet another function is to advise the Government on food supply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, SFA can assist the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) to mitigate food price increases by collecting and analysing data on food supply and import prices, conduct research on alternative food supply sources and provide advice on the diversification of food supply sources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A more direct way that SFA can do this is to leverage its close relationship with the food import and distribution businesses here to diversify food supply sources to mitigate food price increases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Compared to MTI, the SFA will be in a better position to do this, given that it will be working closely with stakeholders on the ground and will be the domain expert in understanding our food supply system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In case anyone thinks this is going beyond the natural scope of SFA, I would like to point out that the Agency is housed under the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources (MEWR), together with NEA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NEA has been managing our hawker centres and has been concerned with both the food safety and hygiene aspects of our hawker centres as well as ensuring a low-cost avenue of cooked food for Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The function of mitigating the rising cost of living is well in the institutional purview and experience of MEWR and its agencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second function is addressing household food insecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A recently published report of a study of household food insecurity in Singapore by the Lien Centre for Social Innovation at the Singapore Management University warned that we may be underestimating the problem of hunger here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Household food insecurity comes about when a household has problems with economic and physical access to enough food for a healthy life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Though the study is limited by the small sample size of 236 households and a non-random targeted sampling, it suggests that there are significant pockets of food insecurity in a country that has topped the Global Food Security Index.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a disconcerting finding and warrants a more thorough investigation by the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SFA is well-placed to do this and, I argue, it is obliged to do it, as the Agency's second function stated in clause 5(b) reads, "to support regulation of the handling and supply of food to ensure that it is safe and suitable for human consumption and to promote public health".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, surely, the problem of household food insecurity is well within the scope of the Agency's function to regulate the supply of food to promote public health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Lien Centre researchers also interviewed the representatives of 35 organisations that provided food support to Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two of the recommendations were, one, greater coordination of food support organisations and more effective targeting of food support and, two, prioritising nutritious and quality food.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, given the SFA's would-be close links with food supply businesses and its knowledge of the supply chain networks, the Agency is well-placed to develop the national food support system to fight hunger in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Agency can connect the food support organisations with the food supply chain, and to help the food support organisations coordinate their efforts as well as to provide the organisations with a good supply of excess nutritious and quality food from the supply chain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means the Agency will know and be well-placed to identify the excess stores of food that can be supplied to food support organisations for the national food support system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rising food prices feed into the perception as well as the experience of the increasing cost of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SFA is in a good position to mitigate rising food prices and we should not waste the opportunity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, hunger has no place in Singapore, even if it is just small pockets of households facing food insecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, SFA is in a good position to address this issue and it should.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I shall focus, in particular, on food waste today.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Food waste comprises avoidable food waste and unavoidable food waste.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the following sections, I am referring to avoidable food waste.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's current food supply chain is a linear economy which is the cause of much food waste every day because it is simpler and cheaper for businesses and individuals to throw away food than channel the same to better use.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I was heartened by Minister Masagos' acknowledgement of this fact at the launch of Singapore's Year Towards Zero Waste, where he noted the need for Singapore to adopt a circular economy approach to achieve zero waste.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A circular economy is one where the "waste" of one part of the food cycle becomes resources for another.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While it is important to ensure enough food for Singapore, how can we make sure that we do not over-import food that leads to much waste?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Next on the food chain is avoidable waste generated by businesses, including food manufacturers, food wholesalers and F&B businesses.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While no official numbers have been released, an informal group, like SG Food Rescue, can give us some indication.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: SG Food Rescue rescued over 100 tonnes of food in the past year through volunteer efforts alone.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Less than $5,000 was spent to collect and redistribute the food by 250 individuals to feed 550 people, three meals a day for a whole year.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Remember that this is just one group's effort.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An easier way to understand what 800,000 tonnes of total avoidable food waste a year means is to look at someone like Ah Hua whom I happened to meet at Kreta Ayer a few weeks ago.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In his 50s, partially blind and likely intellectually-challenged, he was not asking for money but for food.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Ah Hua is one of the 400,000 food-insecure people in Singapore, according to Singapore Against Poverty, who need 438 million meals a year.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Eight hundred thousand tonnes of edible food waste translates to 486 million meals a year which would, therefore, allow us to more than provide for everyone who struggles with food security.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Too simplistic a calculation I admit, but I hope we get the point here.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: NEA's current food waste management strategies expressly state that the most preferred methods for food waste management are: one, prevent and reduce food wastage at its source, and two, redistribute unsold and excess food.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In food resource management, the order of priority should be, first, to feed humans, then animals, then to "feed" the soil via composting or as we call it, recycling, before finally generating energy from food waste.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, we seem to manage food waste by doubling down on recycling food waste and recovering energy from food waste, and not enough is done to reduce food waste from upstream sources.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: All edible food waste can and should be redistributed to people like Ah Hua instead of investing millions of dollars to build digesters to turn food waste into energy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The benefit here is not merely reduced waste, but a long-term reduction of the inflated cost of food resource which worsens food insecurity for the poorest amongst us.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, regulations should clearly define terms used in the sale of food, such as "best before", "consume by", "sell by", "use by" and "expiry" dates.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Presently, these terms denoting dates all have the same meaning, which is, that businesses are not legally allowed to sell an item past the indicated date.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, if some of these terms, in fact, only denote the food manufacturer's recommended period of consumption for the food items sold, then regulations can be enacted to extend the shelf life of, for instance, processed foods on the condition that the food is donated to charities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This allows for food to be redistributed instead of being discarded.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, and I acknowledge that this might be controversial, the law should make it costly for businesses to throw away edible food.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Donating food which remains edible but is no longer retailable costs time and manpower.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses, therefore, prefer to discard food because it is cheaper and more convenient to do so.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Policies which disincentivise edible food wastage will push businesses to seek alternatives.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In France, a law was enacted in 2016 exactly for this.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The enactment of such regulations certainly requires much preparatory legwork, such as better measurement and reporting of how much food is discarded, so commissioning a continuous collection and study of data concerning food waste would be most important and relevant to clause 5(1)(n) of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: After all, if we cannot measure something, we cannot improve it.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Another step could be to legislate that all food imported or grown in Singapore has to be sold or donated, with a similar concept to the Extended Producer Responsibility that is coming into effect for e-waste.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given that such a policy would be controversial, it should be accompanied by a third complementary measure: a law which incentivises businesses to donate food to charity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This could come in the form of tax rebates from food donations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Ideally, the charities which receive food donations should be the ones to weigh the donations received and provide receipts to the businesses for their food donations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We know that we will not be able to feed future population growth if the world continues to produce and consume food the way we currently do.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, research is also showing that with changing air quality, concentration of carbon dioxide as well as soil quality, the levels of nutrition in our staple foods could change drastically.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This dual challenge requires radical re-imagination of the world's food production systems.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: New farming techniques, plant-based meats, alternative protein, all these developments require adaptable food regulations that allow for rapid adoption without compromising on food safety considerations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Such a system is already present in the UK; (b) being flexible to react quickly to changing technology and norms when it comes to food labelling and food risks assessments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Transparency around supply chains and, therefore, confidence in terms of food safety, can be achieved through increasingly low-cost technology.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We can learn much from our own history.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When we gained Independence, we harnessed our limited resources to save every single drop across our national water taps because every drop counts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We can learn much from the rainforest that wastes none.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It shall be with this same wisdom, creativity and kampung spirit involving all sectors of society – from the Public Service to businesses to civil societies, and every single consumer, that we collectively ensure Ah Hua's and our next generation's food security is assured.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I also note our success thus far to keep swine flu out of our food supply.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The creation of SFA also offers economic opportunities for our food manufacturing and supply industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is a trust deficit in food, especially in developing Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Most Asian customers do not fully trust the industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, where there are many international standards for food, both at a general and industry level, these standards are usually: one, not well understood by customers; two, too narrowly defined.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, the important Good Manufacturing Process standard does not provide end-to-end assurance of food products; and three, not well enforced.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many companies work hard to get a certification but fail to keep up with these standards subsequently.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As Asia grows, consumers, especially those within developing Asia, desires high-quality food, such as milk powder that are free from contamination.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are also well-to-do consumers who also want organic food, food produced using fair trade principles and food produced without adversely impacting the environment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Leading food manufacturing companies tried to position themselves as such.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
